air-pollution: Air pollutants are primary (released directly: CO, NOx, SO2, particulates, VOCs) or secondary (formed in the air: ozone near the ground, sulfuric and nitric acid). Coal burning is the main source of SO2 and mercury; hot combustion makes NOx; CO starves the blood of oxygen; PM2.5 reaches deep into the lungs. The Clean Air Act sets limits on six criteria pollutants.
photochemical-smog: Photochemical smog is a mix of secondary pollutants, mainly ground-level ozone, made when nitrogen oxides and VOCs react in sunlight. NO from morning traffic becomes NO2; sunlight splits NO2, and the freed oxygen atom forms ozone, which VOCs help build up. Ozone peaks in the early afternoon on hot, sunny days, irritates lungs and damages plants, and falls after dark.
thermal-inversion: A thermal inversion is a layer of warm air over cooler air near the ground, the reverse of the normal pattern. The cool, dense air cannot rise through the warm layer, so smoke, exhaust and particles build up near the ground. Inversions form on clear, calm nights and winter mornings and in valleys and basins, and they break when the sun warms the ground or wind mixes the air.
co2-particulates: Carbon dioxide and particulate matter have natural sources as well as human ones. Volcanoes, wildfires, respiration and decomposition release CO2, though human emissions are now about 100 times volcanic ones. Volcanic ash, wildfire smoke, desert dust, sea spray and pollen add particles. Particles scatter and absorb light, causing haze, and fine particles harm the lungs whatever their source.
indoor-air: Indoor air pollutants include radon from uranium in rock, formaldehyde and other VOCs off-gassed by new materials, carbon monoxide from poorly burning stoves and furnaces, asbestos fibers from disturbed old insulation, and smoke from cooking over open fires. Tight buildings trap them. Testing, ventilation, removing the source and CO detectors reduce the harm.
reducing-air-pollutants: Air pollutants are cut by using cleaner fuel, burning it better, or capturing pollutants after burning. Scrubbers remove SO2; electrostatic precipitators and baghouse filters remove particles; catalytic converters change CO, NOx and hydrocarbons into less harmful gases; vapor recovery nozzles capture gasoline vapor. Laws such as emission caps and cap-and-trade programs make these cuts happen. None of the devices removes CO2.
acid-rain: Acid deposition forms when sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxides from power plants and vehicles react in the air to make sulfuric and nitric acid, which fall in rain, snow and fog or as dry particles, often far downwind. Each drop of 1 in pH is ten times more acidic. It acidifies lakes, harms fish and forests, and dissolves stone; limestone buffers it. Cutting SO2 and NOx raised rain pH.
noise-pollution: Noise pollution is sound that harms people or wildlife because of its level or timing. It is measured in decibels, a logarithmic scale where each 10 dB is 10 times the intensity, and long exposure above about 85 dB damages hearing. Noise also raises stress in people and masks the sounds animals use to mate, feed and migrate. Barriers, quieter machines, slower ships, hearing protection and rules reduce it.
pollution-sources: Point sources release pollution from one identifiable place, such as a pipe or smokestack, so they can be measured, permitted and treated. Nonpoint sources, such as runoff from farms, lawns and streets, come from many diffuse places. Laws have cut point sources sharply, so nonpoint pollution is now the largest share, and it is reduced by changing how land is used.
human-impacts-ecosystems: Pollution changes ecosystems by pushing conditions outside species' tolerance ranges. Indicator species such as mayfly larvae reveal water quality. Heat stress bleaches corals by making them expel their algae; sediment smothers reefs; oil spills coat and poison wildlife; and plastics entangle animals and break into microplastics that enter food webs.
endocrine-disruptors: Endocrine disruptors are chemicals that interfere with hormones by mimicking them, blocking their receptors or changing how much is made. Atrazine, BPA, phthalates and synthetic estrogens are examples. Even at very low doses they can cause intersex fish, abnormal frog development and human reproductive and developmental problems. Limits on use, extra cleaning steps at wastewater plants and safe medicine disposal reduce them.
wetlands-mangroves: Wetlands and mangroves provide valuable ecosystem services: they store floodwater, recharge groundwater, filter pollutants, store carbon, buffer coasts against storm surge and shelter fish and birds. Draining and filling them for development and farms, and clearing mangroves for shrimp ponds, removes these services, raising flood and storm damage and lowering water quality. Permits, mitigation and restoration protect them.
eutrophication: Cultural eutrophication happens when nitrogen and phosphorus from fertilizer, manure and sewage enter water. The extra nutrients feed an algal bloom that shades plants below; when the algae and plants die, decomposers use oxygen to break them down, dissolved oxygen falls, and fish and bottom animals die in hypoxic dead zones. Keeping nutrients on the land and out of water prevents it.
thermal-pollution: Thermal pollution is heat added to water by people, mostly from power plant and factory cooling water and from warm runoff. Warmer water holds less dissolved oxygen while raising the oxygen needs of fish, so cold-water species decline, and sudden changes cause thermal shock. Cooling towers and ponds, shade along streams and temperature limits reduce it.
persistent-organic-pollutants: Persistent organic pollutants are synthetic, carbon-based chemicals such as DDT, PCBs and dioxins that resist breakdown, dissolve in fat, travel long distances on wind and water and stay toxic for decades. They collect in cold regions and in animal fat, harming reproduction and development; DDT thinned the eggshells of birds of prey. Bans such as the Stockholm Convention cut new inputs, but levels fall slowly.
bioaccumulation-biomagnification: Bioaccumulation is the build-up of a persistent, fat-soluble pollutant in one organism over its life. Biomagnification is the rise in its concentration at each higher trophic level, because each consumer eats many organisms and keeps their stored pollutant. DDT, PCBs and methylmercury reach their highest levels in top predators, thinning eggshells in birds of prey and leading to fish advisories for people.
solid-waste: Municipal solid waste in the United States is mostly landfilled (about half in 2018), with the rest recycled, composted or burned. Sanitary landfills use liners, leachate collection, soil cover, gas wells and caps to contain trash; buried organic waste decomposes slowly without oxygen and makes methane. Incineration cuts volume but releases air pollutants and ash. E-waste needs special handling, and ocean dumping is banned.
waste-reduction: Waste is reduced by following the hierarchy: reduce first (less packaging, durable goods), then reuse, then recycle and compost, then recover energy, with landfilling last. Recycling saves materials and energy but has costs; composting turns food and yard waste into soil and avoids landfill methane. Policies such as pay-as-you-throw, bag fees and deposits shift behavior, and landfill gas can generate electricity.
sewage-treatment: Sewage treatment cleans wastewater in stages. Primary treatment physically removes solids as sludge; secondary treatment uses microbes in aerated tanks to break down dissolved organic matter and cut BOD; tertiary treatment removes nitrogen and phosphorus; disinfection kills germs. Sludge is digested and disposed of or reused. Septic systems treat wastewater for single homes, and combined sewers can overflow in storms.
lethal-dose-50: LD50 is the dose, in milligrams per kilogram of body mass, that kills half of a test population; it is read off a graph of percent killed against dose at the 50% line. The lower the LD50, the more toxic the substance. Multiply the LD50 by a body mass to get a whole-body dose, writing the units so kilograms cancel, and convert milligrams to grams when asked.
dose-response-curve: A dose-response curve shows the percent of a test group responding at each dose. It is flat at zero below the threshold dose, rises steeply through 50% and levels off near 100%. Read across from 50% and down to find the LD50 (deaths) or ED50 (another effect). The substance whose curve rises at lower doses is more toxic, and harm can begin far below the LD50.
pollution-human-health: Linking a pollutant to a disease is hard because people face many exposures over long times. Synergism means pollutants together can do more harm than their effects added. Acute effects follow short, high exposures; chronic effects follow long ones. Know ground-level ozone and lung function, asbestos and mesothelioma, and sewage-contaminated water and dysentery.
pathogens: Pathogens are bacteria, viruses, protozoa, fungi and worms that cause infectious diseases. They spread through water, air, food, contact and vectors such as mosquitoes and fleas. Poor sanitation and crowding speed the spread, which is why clean water and sewage treatment prevent cholera. A warming climate can widen the range of vectors and the diseases they carry.
